result: Immunophenotyping of antigen-naïve Kymice demonstrates full B-cell development competence with appropriate frequencies of all major B-cell subpopulations. Memory B cells (6.60% ± 2.51%), germinal center B cells (0.18% ± 0.26%), and plasma cells (0.90% ± 0.28%) were detected at low but consistent frequencies across animals, reflecting lack of immune exposure.
evaluation: Claims C49-C52 provide specific quantitative measurements from flow cytometry (Figure 1), and C51 confirms consistency across animals. The low frequencies of activated B-cell populations (C108) are appropriately interpreted as reflecting antigen-naïve status. The conclusion of full B-cell development competence (C3, C106, C107) is well-supported by the detection of all expected B-cell subpopulations at appropriate frequencies.

result: Kymice exhibit an Igκ/Igλ ratio of 51:49, which is considerably closer to the human ratio (60:40) than the mouse ratio (95:5). This was measured from 3,175 paired VH and VL sequences from naïve B cells.
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 provide established knowledge and measured data for the Igκ/Igλ ratios across species. The Kymouse ratio (51:49) is clearly intermediate and closer to human (60:40) than mouse (95:5), supporting C59. The sample size (3,175 sequences) is adequate for this measurement.

result: IGHV gene usage differs significantly between Kymice and humans, with Kymice showing increased IGHV3 (66.4% vs 44.8% in paired data; 51.6% vs 39.7% in bulk data) and IGHV6 usage, but decreased IGHV1 and IGHV4 usage. These differences are consistent across both paired single-cell and bulk sequencing datasets.
evaluation: Claims C60-C63 and C74-C75 provide specific quantitative measurements from both paired (Figure 2A) and bulk (Figure 3B) sequencing data. The consistency between the two independent datasets strengthens the finding. Statistical significance is indicated in the figures, though specific p-values are not always provided in the claims.

result: IGHJ gene usage shows significant differences between Kymice and humans, with Kymice preferentially using IGHJ6 (39.3% vs 24.5% in paired data; 32.8% vs 28.9% in bulk data) and IGHJ4 (46.7% vs 42.6% in bulk data), while using IGHJ5 and IGHJ1 less frequently.
evaluation: Claims C64, C76, and C77 provide specific measurements from both paired (Figure 2C) and bulk (Figure 3C) sequencing data. However, there is some inconsistency between datasets - IGHJ6 usage difference is more pronounced in paired data than bulk data, suggesting potential sampling or technical variation.

result: IGHD gene subgroup usage differs significantly between Kymice and humans, with human repertoires preferring IGHD2, IGHD4, and IGHD5 subgroups, while Kymouse repertoires preferentially use IGHD1, IGHD6, and IGHD7 subgroups.
evaluation: Claims C78 and C79 provide specific quantitative measurements from bulk VH sequencing data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The differences are substantial (e.g., IGHD1: 24.2% vs 10.3%) and consistent with the overall pattern of differential gene usage.

result: Kymice have CDRH3 lengths intermediate between mice and humans. Mean CDRH3 length is 14.3 amino acids in Kymice compared to 16.6 amino acids in humans and 12.4 amino acids in C57BL/6 mice. Kymouse CDRH3 loops are on average 2.36aa shorter than humans (95% CI: 2.26, 2.48; p<0.001).
evaluation: Claims C80-C84 provide specific quantitative measurements with confidence intervals and p-values from bulk VH sequencing data (Figure 4A). The finding is consistent across both paired (C65) and bulk (C80-C84) datasets. Statistical analysis is rigorous with appropriate confidence intervals.

result: The shorter CDRH3 length in Kymice compared to humans is primarily due to reduced nucleotide insertions at VD and DJ junctions (7.33 fewer nucleotides on average) and differential IGHD gene usage (2.34nt shorter). IGHV and IGHJ gene usage contribute minimally (0.14nt and 0.85nt respectively).
evaluation: Claims C85-C90 provide detailed statistical analysis with confidence intervals and p-values for each contributing factor (Figure 4B). The decomposition analysis is methodologically sound, identifying junctional insertions as the primary driver. C91 and C111 appropriately synthesize these findings.

result: A significantly greater proportion of Kymouse sequences lack junctional insertions compared to humans: 19.1% lack VD insertions (vs 8.2% in humans), 14.1% lack DJ insertions (vs 4.5% in humans), and 3.8% lack both (vs 0.3% in humans).
evaluation: Claims C69-C71 provide specific quantitative measurements from paired sequencing data. The differences are substantial and consistent with the overall finding of reduced junctional diversification in Kymice. However, the manuscript does not provide statistical tests or confidence intervals for these specific proportions.

result: Kymice show reduced CDRH3 diversity at longer lengths and greater repertoire overlap between individuals compared to humans. On average, 5.1% of CDRH3s are shared between Kymice (vs 0.12% between humans), and clonotype sharing is 7.92% (vs 0.84% in humans). This reduced diversity is attributed to fewer junctional insertions.
evaluation: Claims C92-C97 provide specific measurements from overlap analysis (Figure 5G-H). The >25-fold difference in CDRH3 sharing (C95) is substantial. Claims C112-C113 appropriately link this to reduced junctional diversification, supported by citation to Jaffe et al., 2022 (C114). The diversity analysis at different CDRH3 lengths (Figure 5E-F) supports the length-dependent effect.

result: Kymouse naïve BCR repertoires are more human-like than mouse-like in their predicted distribution of CDRH3 structural shapes. The majority of structural clusters used by Kymouse (55.0%) and human (57.5%) repertoires are of human origin, while mouse repertoires predominantly use murine-origin clusters (64.0%). Hierarchical clustering shows Kymouse and human repertoires form a monophyletic cluster separate from mice.
evaluation: Claims C98-C102 provide specific measurements from structural annotation analysis (Figure 6). The structural similarity is demonstrated through multiple approaches: template origin analysis (C98-C100), distance measurements (C101), and hierarchical clustering (C102). Claims C118-C121 provide appropriate interpretation. However, the analysis is limited to CDRH3 lengths 4-16, which may bias results.

result: Using the Hu-mAb humanness scoring tool, 100% of Kymouse and human heavy chain sequences were classified as human, with maximum humanness scores assigned to 98.3% of Kymouse and 99.1% of human sequences. No murine sequences were classified as human.
evaluation: Claims C103-C105 provide clear quantitative results from the humanness scoring analysis. The tool successfully distinguishes mouse sequences (0% classified as human) from Kymouse and human sequences (100% classified as human), validating the humanness of Kymouse sequences. The methodology is appropriate and results are unambiguous.

result: The combined sequence and structural analysis indicates that the naïve Kymouse BCR repertoire is diverse with key similarities to human repertoires, and the structural templates available for antigen binding are human-like.
evaluation: Claims C7, C131, and C132 represent synthesis conclusions drawn from the combined findings. These are well-supported by the multiple lines of evidence presented: immunophenotyping (C3, C8), sequence diversity analysis (C5), structural analysis (C6, C98-C102), and humanness scoring (C103-C105). The conclusions appropriately integrate the various analyses.

result: Kymouse repertoires show a preference for shorter IGHD genes, a pattern also observed in OmniRat BCR repertoires, suggesting this may be common across transgenic rodent platforms.
evaluation: Claim C115 is supported by the IGHD gene usage data (C78-C79, C86). Claim C116 is appropriately qualified as speculation ('may be common') and is supported by comparison to published OmniRat data (Joyce et al., 2020). However, this is based on only two transgenic platforms, limiting the generalizability.

result: Different germline gene distributions in the Kymouse may affect how representative transgenic models are of immune responses to germline-targeting immunogens, especially if desired naïve BCR frequencies are lower than in humans.
evaluation: Claim C117 is appropriately qualified as speculation ('may affect') and is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019. However, this is a forward-looking statement about potential implications rather than a demonstrated result. The manuscript does not provide experimental evidence testing this hypothesis.

result: Kymice contain the Ig haplotype of a single human subject, and given differences in germline gene usage, the BCR response to antigen stimulus in Kymouse likely represents only a subset of the possible diversity of the outbred human response.
evaluation: Claim C122 is a factual description of the Kymouse genetic engineering. Claim C123 is established knowledge supported by citation to Rodriguez et al., 2022. Claim C124 is a logical inference from C122 and C123, appropriately qualified as 'likely.' The conclusion is reasonable but represents speculation about future immune responses rather than demonstrated results.

result: The less diverse primary repertoire of the Kymouse does not appear to be an impediment to its use as a source of high-affinity therapeutic antibodies, and a higher frequency of shorter CDRH3 lengths could be favorable for developability.
evaluation: Claim C125 is an inference not directly tested in this study, though it is consistent with prior successful use of Kymouse for antibody discovery (C127-C130). Claim C126 is speculation supported by citation to Raybould et al., 2019 regarding developability. Neither claim is directly supported by data in this manuscript - they represent interpretations of implications rather than demonstrated results.

result: Immunoglobulin loci-transgenic animals are widely used in antibody discovery and vaccine response modeling. The first Ig transgenic mouse was created in 1989, with complete human Ig haplotype integration achieved in 2014. As of April 2022, 20 of 127 therapeutic antibodies licensed in the US or EU were derived from transgenic mouse platforms.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 represent established knowledge about the field. Claims C9-C11 are historical facts supported by appropriate citations (Brüggemann et al., 1989; Lee et al., 2014) and database evidence (Thera-SAbDab). These provide important context but are not novel findings of this study.

result: The Kymouse genetic engineering involves insertion of complete human V, D, and J genes at endogenous mouse loci while retaining mouse constant regions. Previous work (Lee et al., 2014) showed Kymice exhibit normal B-cell production and maturation with diverse BCRs showing human-like CDRH3 lengths and somatic hypermutation.
evaluation: Claims C12-C15 describe the Kymouse genetic engineering, which is established knowledge. Claims C16-C19 cite prior work (Lee et al., 2014) characterizing Kymouse B-cell development. These are appropriately cited background claims that provide context for the current study but are not novel findings.

result: Background knowledge about B-cell development, immunoglobulin genetics, and BCR repertoire sequencing methodology is established. This includes B-cell maturation pathways, germinal center formation, antibody structure, V(D)J recombination, and repertoire analysis approaches.
evaluation: Claims C20-C48 represent established immunological and methodological knowledge, appropriately cited where relevant. These provide necessary background context but are not novel findings of this study. They establish the conceptual framework for interpreting the experimental results.

result: High-throughput sequencing recovered 3,175 paired VH/VL sequences and 451,655 unpaired VH sequences from 22 Kymice. At enhanced depth, all IGHD and IGHJ genes in the Kymouse haplotype and all non-orphon IGHD and IGHJ genes in humans were observed in all repertoires.
evaluation: Claims C53-C54 and C72-C73 describe the sequencing data obtained and gene coverage achieved. These are methodological results demonstrating adequate sampling depth. The complete coverage of IGHD and IGHJ genes validates the comprehensiveness of the sequencing approach.

result: There was no significant difference in CDRL3 length between humans and Kymice (average 9.8aa ± 0.002 vs 9.7aa ± 0.2) in the paired sequencing data.
evaluation: Claim C66 reports a negative result from the paired sequencing data (Figure 2F). The similar CDRL3 lengths contrast with the CDRH3 length differences, suggesting the light chain is less affected by the differences in junctional diversification. The standard errors suggest adequate precision.

result: Previous studies have used Kymouse for immunizations with various antigens, demonstrating functional polyclonal serum responses and monoclonal antibodies that bind physiologically important epitopes equivalent to those found in humans.
evaluation: Claims C127-C130 cite multiple prior studies demonstrating successful use of Kymouse for antibody discovery and vaccine response modeling. These provide important validation context but are not novel findings of this study. The citations support the utility of the platform despite the repertoire differences identified.
